entities.summary:
Johann Georg Gödelmann (1559–1611) stands as a pivotal German jurist, diplomat, and demonological writer whose work significantly shaped legal discourse during the zenith of early modern witch trials. Born in Tuttlingen, Württemberg, and later serving prominently in Rostock and Dresden, Gödelmann navigated the complex intellectual currents of the late 16th century, meticulously applying Roman-canonical legal principles to the highly charged accusations of witchcraft, thereby influencing the gradual shift towards more rigorous evidential standards in a period rife with fear and persecution.

His academic career flourished at the University of Rostock, where he became a professor of law and served multiple terms as rector. Beyond academia, Gödelmann engaged in diplomatic service for the Duke of Mecklenburg, showcasing his practical legal acumen. His most enduring contribution, however, remains his seminal treatise, *De magis, veneficis et lamiis* (On Magicians, Poisoners, and Witches), published in 1591. In this work, Gödelmann critically examined the legal procedures surrounding witchcraft accusations, advocating strongly against the use of torture without substantial evidence and insisting on the strict application of established legal norms, including the presumption of innocence, even for alleged witches.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Johann Georg Gödelmann was a key figure in the legal debate surrounding early modern witch trials, whose influential treatise *De magis* (1591) significantly advanced arguments for stricter evidence and due process, contributing to the intellectual foundation for the eventual decline of mass witch hunts.
